questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: The hypothesis a research question implies
questions.learningObjective: State the testable hypothesis implied by a design-brief research question.
questions.stem: A design brief asks whether adding a stiffening rib to a gearbox bracket lowers peak vibration during a 12 Hz shaker sweep. Which statement states the hypothesis the question implies?

options.text: H1: ribbed brackets reach lower peak vibration than baseline brackets, with H0 predicting equal peaks.
Only H0 exists, because the question is neutral and states no alternative direction at all.
options.misconception: Thinks a research question can only state a null hypothesis.

options.text: H1: ribbed brackets differ from baseline in peak vibration, with no direction specified.
options.misconception: Reads a directional question as a two-sided comparison.

options.text: H1: the baseline bracket is stiffer than the ribbed bracket in every frequency band tested.
options.misconception: Invents a stiffness claim the brief never asks about.

questions.explanation: The wording whether ... lowers anticipates a direction, so the implied alternative is lower peak vibration with a null of no difference. A neutral question would leave the direction unspecified.
questions.hint: Look for directional wording in the brief.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Null and alternative that exhaust the outcome space
questions.learningObjective: Construct a null and alternative pair that partitions the entire outcome space.

stimulus.body: The damper housing team must decide whether a new elastomer ring changes the decay ratio of the assembly rig. A supplier claims a 12 percent reduction in ring-down time. The brief asks the analyst to test that claim at the 5 percent level and to report whether the data support it.

questions.stem: Using the damper housing brief, which null and alternative pair leaves no outcome unassigned?

options.text: H0: mean ring-down time differs by 12 percent from the current elastomer; H1: it does not.
options.misconception: Puts a specific 12 percent effect in the null hypothesis.

options.text: H0: the new elastomer changes mean ring-down time; H1: the change is exactly zero.
options.misconception: Puts the substantive effect in the null hypothesis.

options.text: H0: the new elastomer changes mean ring-down time; H1: it leaves mean ring-down time unchanged.
H0: mean ring-down time is unchanged; H1: mean ring-down time increases beyond the baseline.
options.misconception: Covers only one direction of a possible change.

questions.explanation: A null of no change and an alternative of any change cover every possible outcome exactly once. B empties the null, and D covers only one direction, leaving outcomes unassigned.
questions.hint: The two hypotheses must partition all outcomes.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a pooled-variance t test actually assumes
questions.learningObjective: State the variance and normality conditions behind a pooled-variance two-sample t test.
questions.stem: A fixture supplier compares mean bore diameter between two machining lots using a pooled-variance two-sample t test. Which condition must hold for that test's pooled variance estimate to be valid?

options.text: Both lots must come from the same machine and be measured with the same instrument.
options.misconception: Believes only reproducibility of measurement matters.

options.text: The two lot variances must be roughly comparable and the data in each lot approximately normal.
Each lot must contain at least thirty measurements so the central limit theorem applies.
options.misconception: Assumes a sample size threshold replaces normality.

options.text: The two lot means must be close enough that the pooled standard error stays small.
options.misconception: Assumes pooling validity depends on the means being close.

questions.explanation: Pooling assumes one common variance for both groups, and unequal variances inflate type I error. Approximate normality within each group keeps the t distribution an accurate reference for the standardised difference.
questions.hint: Pooling is about spread, not about sample size.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: The distributional assumption behind a one-way analysis of variance
questions.learningObjective: Identify the residual and variance assumptions of a one-way analysis of variance.
questions.stem: Four curing-agent formulations are tested for 28-day compressive strength, giving means of 41, 44, 39, and 45 MPa. An analyst runs a one-way analysis of variance and reports a p-value of 0.02. Which statement about the underlying distributional assumption is correct?

options.text: The p-value is valid only if each group is normal with a common variance.
The p-value is valid only if the four sample means are normally distributed.
options.misconception: Confuses normality of means with normality of readings.

options.text: The p-value is valid only if the residuals across all formulations are exactly zero.
options.misconception: Believes a zero-residual design is what the analysis needs.

options.text: The p-value is valid only if the four formulations were sampled in random order.
options.misconception: Believes run order is the distributional assumption.

questions.explanation: The analysis models each group as normal with a shared variance, and the F test relies on normality of the residuals. Normality of the four sample means plays no part in the assumption.
questions.hint: Think about the errors around each group mean.

questions.topic: When a rank-based test is the required choice

questions.stem: A geoteam records ultrasonic pulse velocity for concrete cores from a dam gallery. The readings are heavily right-skewed with two clear outliers caused by a miscalibrated transducer. Which test does the brief require?

options.text: A Mann-Whitney rank test, because the skew and outliers break the normality a t test needs.
A pooled two-sample t test, because outliers cancel out in the mean when sample sizes match.
options.misconception: Assumes averaging removes the effect of outliers.

options.text: A one-way analysis of variance, because it is more robust than a t test for small samples.
options.misconception: Assumes analysis of variance tolerates severe skew.

options.text: A paired t test, because cores from the same gallery location are naturally matched pairs.
options.misconception: Assumes proximity automatically creates valid pairs.

questions.explanation: Strong skew and extreme outliers violate the conditions a t test relies on, so a rank test is sound here. Analysis of variance tolerates skew no better, and unverified pairing adds an assumption.

questions.stem: A calibration lab wants to know whether a new torque wrench cell reads high relative to a certified 10 N m reference. The reference reading is known with negligible uncertainty, and each of 25 trials uses the same cell. Which analysis and framing is correct?

options.text: A two-sample t test against the reference, since the reference value must vary between trials to be a sample.
options.misconception: Believes a known constant must be treated as a second sample.

options.text: A one-sample t test of the cell readings against the fixed reference value, because the reference is a known constant.
A paired t test, because each trial reading forms a pair with the certified reference value.

options.misconception: Prefers internal history over the certified reference.

questions.explanation: Only the cell readings vary, since the certified reference is a known constant, so this is a one-sample comparison against a fixed benchmark. Treating the constant as a second sample fabricates variability.
questions.hint: Ask which quantity actually varies.

questions.learningObjective: State what a paired design supports for a correlation between two readings.
questions.stem: A bearing team measures vibration amplitude and then bearing temperature on the same rig at each of twelve test points. Which relationship does this paired design actually support?

options.text: A correlation valid only if the two readings at each point belong to the same physical unit.
A correlation valid whenever both readings are recorded on the same day by the same technician.
options.misconception: Confuses shared conditions with genuine pairing.

options.text: A correlation valid because the two variables are measured on a common numeric scale.

questions.explanation: A paired design supports a within-unit correlation, so both readings must describe the same physical unit or event. Shared staffing only removes nuisance variation, and a common scale does not create pairing.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Null and alternative that exhaust the outcome space
questions.learningObjective: Explain why hypotheses must be exhaustive and state a valid pair.
questions.stem: A brief asks whether a new alloy reduces brake-disc wear rate. Explain why the null and alternative hypotheses must together be exhaustive, and state the pair you would use for this design brief.

answer.exemplar: The null and alternative must partition the sample space so that every possible outcome of the wear experiment leads to exactly one of them being tested, leaving no gap for a result to fall through. For this brief I would set H0: the new alloy has the same mean wear rate as the current alloy, and H1: the new alloy has a lower mean wear rate, which is one-sided because the brief asks about a reduction.

questions.explanation: Exhaustiveness guarantees no outcome escapes the test, so a decision always follows. A one-sided alternative matches the reduces wording in the brief and avoids splitting the error rate across two directions.
questions.hint: Think about where a result could otherwise land.

questions.stem: Two machining lots show sample standard deviations of 0.004 mm and 0.012 mm from a pooled-variance comparison. A reviewer asks what the pooled test would have assumed. Which reading of the output is correct?

options.text: The pooled test assumes one common variance, so the threefold spread gap should be checked first.
The pooled test is unaffected by the spread difference because it estimates one variance from both lots.
options.misconception: Believes pooling removes the need to compare variances.

The four bath means are normally distributed and the sample sizes must all be identical.
options.misconception: Confuses normality of means with normality of readings.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: The correlation a paired design assumes
questions.learningObjective: Explain the conclusion a paired correlation supports and its limits.
questions.stem: A turbine team logs inlet temperature and blade vibration on the same 24 rotor positions during one test. Explain what correlation this paired design can support and what it cannot.

answer.exemplar: Because both readings describe the same rotor position at the same moment, the pairing supports a within-position correlation between inlet temperature and vibration amplitude, and its test accounts for the strong position-to-position variation that a two-sample comparison would treat as noise. It cannot establish that temperature causes vibration, nor can it rule out a shared third factor such as blade condition or balance quality, because no random assignment of temperature was performed.

questions.explanation: Pairing removes between-position variation and sharpens a within-position correlation. It describes association only: temperature was not randomly assigned, so no causal claim is licensed.
questions.hint: Ask what the pairing removes and does not license.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a certified benchmark calls for a one-sample analysis.
questions.stem: A brief compares a new solder alloy's joint resistance with a fixed 2.5 milliohm standard. Explain why one-sample and two-sample framings differ here, and state which you would use.

answer.exemplar: A one-sample test compares the mean of the new alloy's readings with the single known value of 2.5 milliohms, because that standard is a fixed constant with no sampling variability of its own. A two-sample test would treat the standard as though it were another set of random measurements drawn from a population, which is false here, and it would consume degree of freedom and add noise for no reason. I would therefore use a one-sample t test against the certified value.

questions.explanation: The distinction is whether the comparison value varies across observations. A certified constant does not, so it belongs in the null as a fixed benchmark and one set of readings forms the sample.
questions.hint: Does the standard vary from trial to trial?

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: The correlation a paired design assumes

questions.stem: A rig logs 18 test articles, each with a baseline and a post-modification reading. If the standard deviation of the paired differences is 4 mm, what is the standard error of the mean paired difference?
questions.explanation: The standard error of a mean difference divides the difference standard deviation by the square root of the pair count, so 4 over the square root of 18 gives about 0.94 mm. Using 36 raw readings would understate the error.
questions.hint: Divide by the square root of the pair count.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: The correlation a paired design assumes
questions.learningObjective: Explain the within-unit conclusion a paired correlation supports.
questions.stem: A field team records flow rate and pressure drop across the same 12 pipe segments. Explain what this paired design supports and what it fails to support.

answer.exemplar: The paired design supports a correlation computed within each segment, so the relationship between flow rate and pressure drop is estimated after removing the large segment-to-segment differences caused by length, diameter, and roughness. That is the informative question when segments vary so much. The design does not support any claim that raising flow causes the pressure drop to change, because flow was observed rather than assigned, and it does not rule out a confounder such as a partially blocked strainer raising pressure drop while the flow controller happens to run lower.

questions.explanation: Pairing removes between-segment variation, so the correlation reflects within-segment association. Because flow was observed rather than assigned, the design cannot support a causal claim.
questions.hint: Ask what the pairing removes and cannot prove.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: When a rank-based test is the required choice
questions.learningObjective: Explain how to handle skewed data with an invalid sensor file.
questions.stem: A road lab compares braking distances on two asphalt mixes, with right-skewed stopping times and one corrupted sensor file. Explain what you would do and why.

answer.exemplar: I would first pull the corrupted sensor file out of the dataset and record why it is unusable, because an equipment fault produces readings that carry no information about either mix. I would then check whether the right skew persists in the remaining stopping times, and if it does I would compare the mixes with a rank-based test, which does not require normally distributed observations, and report the difference in median stopping time with a rank-based interval. I would not delete the upper tail, because the tail may be the physically interesting part of braking behaviour.

questions.explanation: Invalid readings must be excluded with a stated reason, and the remaining skew calls for a method whose assumptions hold rather than a routine parametric test. Trimming the tail would remove the behaviour of interest.
questions.hint: Exclude what is invalid, then match method to shape.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: The distributional assumption behind a one-way analysis of variance
questions.learningObjective: Explain why equal variances matter when reading an analysis of variance.
questions.stem: A refinery compares sulphur content across four crude grades. Explain why the equality-of-variance assumption matters when the analysis of variance reports a significant result.

answer.exemplar: The pooled error term in a one-way analysis of variance is the yardstick against which the differences between grade means are judged, and that pooled term is only meaningful if the four grades have roughly the same spread. If one grade has a much larger spread, the pooled estimate is inflated by that grade, which makes the between-group differences harder to detect and shifts the critical value, so a significant result may reflect a mismatch of assumptions rather than a real difference between grades. I would therefore report the variance comparison alongside the analysis and consider a Welch-type alternative.

questions.explanation: The pooled error term judges the group differences, and it stands in for all four groups only when their spreads are comparable. When they are not, significance can reflect a distorted error term.
questions.hint: The pooled error is the yardstick for the comparison.

questions.stem: A durability lab produces 16 pull-out force readings per finish, with 3 finishes. What is the largest possible rank-sum value for the group with the 16 highest readings, given the ranks run from 1 to 48?
questions.explanation: The 16 highest ranks among 48 are 33 through 48, and their sum is (33 + 48) times 16 divided by 2, giving 680. This is the upper limit of the rank statistic used in a rank comparison.
questions.hint: Add the highest sixteen ranks together.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: One-sample against two-sample comparison
questions.learningObjective: Read the degrees of freedom of a one-sample t test from a reported output.
questions.stem: A calibration lab reports a one-sample t statistic of 2.2 on 19 degrees of freedom against a certified 10 millivolt reference. How should a reviewer read this output?

options.text: The 19 degrees of freedom reflect one estimated mean from 20 readings, and the p-value is near 0.04.
The 19 degrees of freedom reflect two estimated means, so the design was a two-sample comparison.
options.misconception: Believes a one-sample test estimates two means.

options.text: The 19 degrees of freedom reflect 19 paired differences from 19 units, indicating a paired design.
options.misconception: Believes one-sample freedom counts indicate pairing.

options.text: The 19 degrees of freedom reflect the reference measurement, which was repeated 19 times.
options.misconception: Believes the certified reference was resampled.

questions.explanation: With 20 readings and one estimated mean, the degrees of freedom are 20 minus 1 equals 19, and t of 2.2 on 19 degrees of freedom gives a two-sided p-value near 0.04.
questions.hint: Degrees of freedom equal readings minus estimated means.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: The correlation a paired design assumes
questions.learningObjective: State what a within-athlete paired correlation supports.
questions.stem: A coach's rig records sprint time and quadriceps force on the same 20 athletes, once each. What does this paired design support?

options.text: A correlation describing how sprint time and quadriceps force move together within the same athlete.
A correlation that separates the effect of quadriceps force on sprint time for every athlete.
options.misconception: Believes observation establishes a causal effect for each athlete.

options.text: A correlation that proves quadriceps force is the sole determinant of sprint time.
options.misconception: Believes a strong association excludes other factors.

options.text: A correlation computed on the 20 athletes only if both readings are normally distributed.
options.misconception: Believes the analysis type depends on the data shape.

questions.explanation: Because both readings describe the same athlete, the pairing supports a within-athlete correlation and removes between-athlete variation in ability. The design stays descriptive and cannot establish causation.
questions.hint: The pairing is within the same athlete.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: The hypothesis a research question implies
questions.learningObjective: Plan the conversion of a research question into a usable hypothesis pair.
questions.stem: One motors team must turn a research question into a testable hypothesis. Which two-stage plan produces a usable pair?

options.text: Name treatment, outcome, comparison and direction, then state a null of no difference and the alternative.
State the alternative, then name the treatment and outcome only after the data are collected.
options.misconception: Defines the hypothesis after the data exist.

options.text: Collect the survey data first, then read the direction of the result to state the hypothesis.
options.misconception: Reads the hypothesis off the observed result.

options.text: State both hypotheses as no difference, then add a direction to whichever one fails.
options.misconception: Chooses the hypothesis after seeing which one fails.

questions.explanation: A testable hypothesis names treatment, outcome, comparison, and direction before data are seen, and the null and alternative then partition the outcome space. Writing them after results makes the analysis a description.
questions.hint: Specify the design before the data arrive.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Null and alternative that exhaust the outcome space
questions.learningObjective: State the most defensible hypothesis pair for an algorithm comparison.
questions.stem: Production monitoring will test a revised algorithm for false alarms. Which hypothesis statement is the most defensible?

options.text: H0: the revised algorithm gives the same mean false-alarm count; H1: it gives a lower mean count.
H0: the revised algorithm changes the false-alarm count; H1: the count stays exactly the same.
options.misconception: Puts the substantive effect in the null hypothesis.

options.text: H0: the mean false-alarm count is zero on the production stream; H1: the count is greater than zero.
options.misconception: Tests a meaningless zero rather than the comparison of interest.

options.text: H0: the revised algorithm reduces false alarms; H1: the revision has no measurable effect.
options.misconception: States the substantive claim as the null.

questions.explanation: The question asks whether the revision reduces false alarms, so the null is no change in the mean count and the alternative is a lower count. Putting the substantive claim in the null misses the brief.
questions.hint: Put the no-change claim in the null.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a pooled-variance t test actually assumes
questions.learningObjective: Compute the variance ratio used to judge a pooled-variance comparison.
questions.stem: Two broach lots give sample variances of 0.0025 and 0.0100 in square millimetres. What is the variance ratio used when a pooled-variance test compares them?
questions.explanation: The larger sample variance over the smaller gives 0.0100 divided by 0.0025, which is 4. A ratio that far from 1 means the equal-variance assumption behind pooling deserves a closer look.
questions.hint: Divide the larger variance by the smaller.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: The distributional assumption behind a one-way analysis of variance
questions.learningObjective: Explain why residual normality matters when reading an analysis of variance.
questions.stem: A pilot line compares four resin grades for tensile strength. Explain why normality of the residuals matters when reading an analysis of variance.

answer.exemplar: The analysis of variance builds its pooled error term from the deviations of each observation from its group mean, and it assumes those deviations are normally distributed so that the F statistic has the reference distribution the critical value is taken from. If the residuals are badly skewed or heavy-tailed, that reference distribution is wrong, the p-value can be misleading in either direction, and a significant result may be an artefact of a few extreme points dominating a group. I would inspect a residual plot before trusting the p-value and would report a rank-based or resampled check alongside it.

questions.explanation: The F test compares group differences to a pooled error term built from the residuals, and its p-value is calibrated only when those residuals are approximately normal. Skewed residuals can make a p-value misleading.
questions.hint: The F distribution is the reference for the statistic.
